name: ATTINY88-AU
title: ATtiny48/88 8-bit AVR microcontrollers with 4/8 Kbytes in-system programmable Flash
summary: ATtiny48 and ATtiny88 are low-power 8-bit AVR RISC microcontrollers that run most of their 123 instructions in one clock, up to 12 MHz from 4.5 to 5.5 V and down to 1.8 V at 4 MHz. They differ only in memory: 4 or 8 Kbytes of self-programmable Flash and 256 or 512 bytes of SRAM, with 64 bytes of EEPROM in both. On chip are an 8-bit and a 16-bit timer, SPI, an I2C-compatible two-wire interface, a 10-bit ADC with 6 or 8 inputs, an analog comparator, a temperature sensor, a watchdog, a calibrated 8 MHz oscillator, debugWIRE and three sleep modes. ATTINY88-AU is the ATtiny88 in the 32-lead TQFP with 28 I/O lines.
key_figures: 8-bit AVR RISC, 123 instructions, 32 x 8 working registers
8 Kbytes Flash, 64 bytes EEPROM, 512 bytes SRAM
28 in 32-lead TQFP, 32-pad QFN and 32-ball UFBGA; 24 in 28-pin PDIP and 28-pad QFN
Internal 8 MHz calibrated, internal 128 kHz, or external clock 0-12 MHz

circuits.title: External clock drive
circuits.description: A clock signal from outside drives CLKI (PB6) with CKSEL[1:0] = 00, from 0 to 12 MHz, referred to the device ground. The frequency may not change by more than 2% between successive cycles; larger steps need the device held in reset.

circuits.title: TWI bus connection
circuits.description: Every device on the bus joins the same two lines, SDA and SCL, through open-drain drivers; R1 pulls SDA and R2 pulls SCL up to VCC, the only parts the bus needs outside the devices. The ATtiny88 joins with SDA on PC4 and SCL on PC5, and must stay powered for the bus to work. Bus capacitance is limited to 400 pF.

circuits.title: ADC power connections
circuits.description: AVCC is fed from VCC through the LC filter L1 and C1, with C1 returned to the GND pin next to AVCC. The ADC input pins, AVCC, GND and the filter sit over an analog ground plane.

circuits.title: debugWIRE setup
circuits.description: The debugger reaches the device over one line, dW, on the RESET pin, with the device supplied at 1.8 V to 5.5 V and ground shared. No external pull-up is needed; one fitted must be 10 kΩ or more, and no capacitor or other reset source may sit on the line.

circuits.title: Parallel programming signals

operation.text: ATtiny48 and ATtiny88 are low-power CMOS 8-bit AVR RISC microcontrollers. Most instructions take one clock, so throughput comes close to 1 MIPS for each MHz of clock.

General purpose I/O: 24 lines, rising to 28 in the 32-lead TQFP, 32-pad QFN and 32-ball UFBGA. ADC inputs: 6, or 8 in those 32-terminal packages. Port A (PA3:0) exists only in them. The device has 32 working registers, an 8-bit and a 16-bit timer/counter each with compare outputs, interrupt sources inside and outside the chip, a two-wire interface that works a byte at a time, an SPI port, a 10-bit ADC, a watchdog with its own oscillator and three power-saving modes chosen in software.

Idle halts the CPU while timers, ADC, comparator, SPI, TWI and interrupts carry on. ADC Noise Reduction halts the CPU and every I/O module but the ADC to quiet the chip during a conversion. Power-down keeps register contents but stops every function until an interrupt or a hardware reset.
The Flash can be rewritten in the system over SPI, with a standard non-volatile memory programmer, or from a boot program running on the core, which may fetch the new application over any interface.
ATtiny48 and ATtiny88 are the same except for memory: 4K or 8K bytes of Flash and 256 or 512 bytes of SRAM, each with 64 bytes of EEPROM.
Reliability qualification projects that fewer than 1 PPM fail to retain data within 20 years at 85°C, or within 100 years at 25°C.
Typical figures come from simulation and from characterising other AVR parts built on the same process.
AVCC powers PC7, PC5:0 and, in the 32-lead packages, PA1:0; all other I/O pins run from VCC.

Ports A, B, C and D are bidirectional, with a pull-up selectable bit by bit. Ports A and B, PC7 and PC5:0, and PD7:4 have symmetrical drive, sinking and sourcing alike; PD3:0 have high sink capability. An input pulled low externally sources current while its pull-up is on. All port pins go tri-state as soon as a reset starts, without needing a running clock.

The core is a Harvard machine: program and data have separate memories and buses. A one-stage pipeline fetches the next instruction while the current one executes, so an instruction completes every clock. Program memory is in-system reprogrammable Flash.

The 32 x 8-bit registers are each reachable in one cycle: two operands are read, the ALU works on them and the result is written back within a single clock. Arithmetic, logic and bit operations run between registers or between a register and a constant. Registers R26 to R31 pair up as the 16-bit pointers X, Y and Z for indirect data addressing, and Z can also point into Flash for table lookups. The registers also occupy data addresses 0x00 to 0x1F, so a pointer can index any of them.
Most instructions are one 16-bit word; some are 32 bits. Jumps and calls can reach the whole address space.

SREG is updated after every ALU operation to describe the result, which often removes the need for a separate compare. It is not saved on entry to an interrupt routine or restored on return; software must do that.

The stack lives in data SRAM, so its size is bounded only by free SRAM. It grows downward: PUSH decrements the stack pointer by one and POP increments it by one; a call or interrupt pushes a two-byte return address (pointer down by two) and RET or RETI pops it (up by two). Software must set SP in the reset routine before any call or interrupt, to a value no lower than the start of SRAM (0x0100).
The I/O space holds 64 addresses, reachable directly or as data addresses 0x20 to 0x5F. Extended I/O at data addresses 0x60 to 0xFF is reached only with LD/LDS/LDD and ST/STS/STD.

The CPU clock clkCPU comes straight from the selected clock source with no internal division. With parallel fetch and execute and the single-cycle register file, an ALU operation on two registers reads, executes and writes back in one clock, giving up to 1 MIPS per MHz.

Each interrupt has its own vector and enable bit, and also needs the global I bit in SREG. Vectors sit at the bottom of program memory; a lower address means higher priority, RESET first and INT0 next. Taking an interrupt clears I, and RETI sets it again; software may set I inside a handler to allow nesting. Programming lock bits LB2 or LB1 may disable interrupts depending on the program counter.

Flag-type interrupts set a flag that is remembered while the interrupt or the global enable is off, and are served by priority once enabled; hardware clears the flag on entry, and writing one to it clears it too. Level-type interrupts fire only while their condition lasts and may have no flag. After returning from an interrupt, the core always runs one instruction of the main program before serving another pending one. After CLI no interrupt is taken, even one arriving with the CLI itself. After SEI the next instruction runs before any pending interrupt, so SEI followed by SLEEP enters sleep first.

Response to an enabled interrupt takes at least four clocks, during which the program counter is pushed; the vector, normally a jump, adds three more. A multi-cycle instruction in progress finishes first. Waking from sleep adds four clocks on top of the sleep mode's start-up time. Returning with RETI takes four clocks, popping two bytes of program counter, raising SP by two and setting I.

Flash is 4K or 8K bytes of 16-bit words, since every instruction is 16 or 32 bits wide; word addresses run 0x0000 to 0x07FF or 0x0FFF, and the program counter is 11/12 bits wide. Constant tables can be placed anywhere in it and read with LPM; SPM writes it. Endurance is at least 10,000 write/erase cycles.

Data space is 512/768 locations: 32 working registers, 64 I/O registers, 160 extended I/O registers and 256/512 bytes of SRAM. All of it is volatile. Reserved bits should be written as zero and reserved I/O addresses never written. The low 32 I/O registers (0x00 to 0x1F) accept the bit instructions SBI, CBI, SBIC and SBIS. Three general purpose I/O registers, GPIOR0 to GPIOR2, hold any data and accept the bit instructions, which suits flags and global variables.

Five modes reach the volatile memory: direct, which covers the whole data space; indirect; indirect with displacement, up to 63 locations from the base in Y or Z; indirect with pre-decrement; and indirect with post-increment, the last two using X, Y or Z. An SRAM access takes two clkCPU cycles.

64 bytes of EEPROM form a separate data space, read and written a byte at a time through registers in I/O space. Its write timing comes from the internal 8 MHz oscillator, which must be within its calibration limits. Endurance is at least 100,000 write/erase cycles.

Writes are atomic, erasing and writing the byte in one longer operation, or split, with the erase done ahead of time (for example at start-up) so a later write is quick, which helps when the supply is falling. EEPM1:0 in EECR choose the mode. Only one operation may run at a time: poll EEPE or use the EEPROM Ready interrupt (enabled by EERIE).

Read: wait for EEPE to clear, load EEAR with the address, set EERE, then take the byte from EEDR; the CPU stops for four clocks. Erase or write: wait for EEPE to clear, set EEPM1:0, load EEAR (and EEDR for a write), set EEMPE and then, within four clocks, EEPE; the CPU stops for two clocks and EEPE stays set until the operation ends. A location must be erased before it is written, or the data is corrupted. Interrupts should be kept off during these timed sequences.

A supply too low for the EEPROM or for the CPU can corrupt EEPROM contents. Holding the device in reset through low-voltage periods avoids it; the internal brown-out detector does this, or an external low-VCC reset circuit where its levels do not fit. A write already started completes through a reset as long as the supply holds up.

clkCPU drives the core, register file, status register and stack memory. clkI/O drives most I/O modules such as the timers, SPI and external interrupts; some external interrupts and the TWI start-condition detector work asynchronously, so TWI address match operates in every sleep mode. clkFLASH runs the Flash interface, normally together with clkCPU. clkADC has its own domain so the CPU and I/O clocks can stop during a conversion for less noise. clkTWIHS clocks the TWI in high-speed mode and equals the source clock.
The system clock comes from an external clock on CLKI, the calibrated internal 8 MHz oscillator or the internal 128 kHz oscillator, chosen by the CKSEL fuses.

With the external clock selected, CLKI is driven by an outside clock source, and start-up times follow the SUT fuses. A cycle-to-cycle frequency change above 2% can upset the MCU, so larger changes should be made with the device in reset; the system clock prescaler gives safe run-time frequency changes.

The internal oscillator gives about 8.0 MHz with no outside parts, varying with voltage and temperature. At reset the factory calibration value is loaded into OSCCAL; software can rewrite OSCCAL for better accuracy than the factory setting. When it clocks the chip, the watchdog oscillator still runs the watchdog and the reset time-out.
A low-power 128 kHz oscillator, selected with CKSEL = 11. Its frequency shifts with supply voltage, temperature and process.

Devices ship running from the internal 8.0 MHz oscillator with CKDIV8 programmed, giving a 1.0 MHz system clock, with the longest start-up and the time-out enabled: CKSEL = 0b10, SUT = 0b10, CKDIV8 = 0. Any programming interface can then set the clock as wanted.

CLKPR divides the system clock to cut speed and power, with any clock source; it divides clkI/O, clkADC, clkCPU and clkFLASH. Changes are glitch-free and no intermediate frequency exceeds either the old or the new setting. To change it: write CLKPCE to one with the other CLKPR bits zero, then within four cycles write the new CLKPS value with CLKPCE zero, interrupts disabled throughout.
With the CKOUT fuse programmed, the system clock, after the prescaler, appears on CLKO (PB0), also during reset, overriding the pin's normal I/O. Any clock source may be used.

After all other reset sources release, an internal reset holds for a time-out tTOUT, counted on the watchdog oscillator, whose length the SUT and CKSEL fuses set. The time-out does not measure VCC, so it must outlast the supply rise; where that cannot be ensured, a brown-out detector should be used, and with one the time-out can be turned off. Turning it off without brown-out detection is not recommended. A ripple counter then waits a set number of oscillator cycles before releasing reset. From reset both the time-out and the start-up time apply; waking from Power-down only the start-up time does.

Set SE in SMCR and execute SLEEP; SM1:0 pick Idle, ADC Noise Reduction or Power-down. An enabled interrupt wakes the MCU, which stops for four cycles plus the start-up time, runs the handler and carries on after the SLEEP. Register file and SRAM are kept. A reset during sleep restarts from the reset vector. A level interrupt used to wake must be held long enough. Setting SE just before SLEEP and clearing it on waking avoids unintended sleep.

SM1:0 = 00. clkCPU and clkFLASH stop; SPI, comparator, ADC, TWI, timers, watchdog and interrupts keep running, so internal and external interrupts can wake the MCU. Setting ACD in ACSR powers the comparator down to save current if its interrupt is not needed. An enabled ADC starts a conversion on entry.

SM1:0 = 01. clkI/O, clkCPU and clkFLASH stop while the ADC, external interrupts, TWI address watch and watchdog keep running, improving ADC resolution. An enabled ADC starts a conversion on entry. Wake sources: ADC conversion complete, external reset, watchdog reset or interrupt, brown-out reset, TWI address match, EEPROM ready, a low level on INT0 or INT1, or any enabled pin change.

SM1:0 = 10. The external oscillator stops; only asynchronous modules run. Wake sources: external reset, watchdog reset or interrupt, brown-out reset, TWI address match, a low level on INT0 or INT1, or any enabled pin change. The delay between the wake-up condition and wake-up taking effect, which lets the clock restart and settle, is set by the same CKSEL fuses that set the reset time-out.

With the BOD enabled by the BODLEVEL fuses, software can turn it off during Power-down by writing BODS (bit 6 of MCUCR) through a timed sequence; it is off from entering sleep and back on at wake-up, and sleep current falls to the fuse-disabled level. Wake-up then takes as long as a wake from reset. BODS resets to zero, leaving the BOD on.

Disable the ADC before sleeping (it stays on in every sleep mode otherwise, and the first conversion after re-enabling is an extended one). Disable the comparator in Idle if unused and always in ADC Noise Reduction; if it uses the internal reference, disable it in every sleep mode or the reference stays on. The BOD and the watchdog, once enabled, run in all sleep modes and add noticeably to deep-sleep current. The internal reference runs whenever the BOD, the comparator or the ADC needs it and must be given its start-up time after being off. An enabled debugWIRE (DWEN fuse) keeps the main clock running in sleep.

Pins should not drive resistive loads during sleep. Where clkI/O and clkADC are both stopped, the digital input buffers are switched off unless needed for wake-up. A floating input, or one near VCC/2, draws excess current through its buffer; analog inputs should always have their digital buffers disabled through DIDR1 and DIDR0.

Reset returns every I/O register to its initial value and starts the program at the reset vector, which must hold an RJMP to the reset routine. I/O ports go to their reset state at once, with no clock. When the last reset source releases, a delay counter stretches the internal reset for the time-out the SUT and CKSEL fuses set, letting power settle. Unused interrupt vectors may hold ordinary code.

Four sources: power-on reset when VCC is under VPOT or falls fast; external reset from a low on RESET longer than the minimum pulse; watchdog system reset when the watchdog expires in reset mode; brown-out reset when VCC is under VBOT with the BOD enabled. MCUSR flags which one occurred (PORF, EXTRF, BORF, WDRF).

An on-chip detector holds reset while VCC is below its threshold. Once VCC rises past VPOT the delay counter sets how long reset is held; a fall below the detection level reasserts reset at once. RESET may be tied to VCC, or held low externally to extend the start-up.

A low on RESET longer than the minimum pulse width resets the device, clock or no clock; shorter pulses may not. When the pin rises past VRST, the device starts after tTOUT. Programming the RSTDISBL fuse disables the external reset and frees PC6 as I/O, leaving power-on and brown-out reset.

The BOD compares VCC with a trigger level set by the BODLEVEL fuses, with hysteresis. Reset asserts at once when VCC falls below VBOT- and releases tTOUT after VCC rises above VBOT+. A dip shorter than tBOD is not detected.
A watchdog time-out produces a reset pulse one CK long; the time-out period tTOUT starts on its falling edge.

An internal bandgap serves the BOD and can feed the comparator or the ADC. It runs while the BOD is enabled by the BODLEVEL fuses, while ACBG in ACSR connects it to the comparator, or while the ADC is enabled. Without the BOD it needs its start-up time after ACBG is set or the ADC enabled before the comparator or ADC output is trusted. Clearing all three conditions before Power-down turns it off.

The watchdog counts a separate 128 kHz oscillator, with time-outs from 2K to 1024K cycles chosen by WDP3:0. Software restarts it with WDR. Interrupt mode raises an interrupt on expiry (usable to wake from sleep or as a timer), system reset mode resets the device, and interrupt-and-reset mode first interrupts and then switches to reset mode, allowing a safe shutdown. The WDTON fuse, if programmed, forces system reset mode with WDE locked at 1 and WDIE at 0.

To clear WDE or change the time-out: write WDCE and WDE both to one in one operation (WDE must be one whatever its old value), then within four clocks write the wanted WDE and WDP bits with WDCE zero, in one operation. Reset the watchdog before changing WDP, since a shorter period could expire at once.

A watchdog enabled by accident (a runaway pointer or a brown-out, for example) is still enabled after the reset it causes, so software that does not expect it can be held in repeated time-out resets. Clearing WDRF and WDE at start-up, whether or not the watchdog is used, prevents this.

INT0, INT1 and PCINT27:0 trigger even when the pins are outputs, which allows software interrupts. Pin change groups: PCI3 for PCINT27:24, PCI2 for PCINT23:16, PCI1 for PCINT15:8 and PCI0 for PCINT7:0, each pin masked in by PCMSK3 to PCMSK0. Pin changes are detected asynchronously and wake the device from any sleep mode. INT0 and INT1 can trigger on a falling edge, a rising edge, any change or a low level; edges need clkI/O, while a low level fires as long as the pin is held low.

The pin is sampled before edges are detected. An edge or change pulse longer than one clock period always produces an interrupt; shorter ones may not. A low level must last until the current instruction finishes.

Low levels on INT0 and INT1 are detected asynchronously, so they can wake the part from sleep modes other than Idle. To wake from Power-down the level must last until the start-up time ends; if it goes away sooner the MCU still wakes but takes no interrupt and resumes after the SLEEP.

Every port supports true read-modify-write: SBI and CBI change one pin's direction, output value or pull-up without touching the others. Drivers can light LED displays directly. Pull-ups are selectable pin by pin, with a resistance that does not vary with supply. Every pin has protection diodes to VCC and ground. Each port has PORTx (data), DDRx (direction) and PINx (input, read-only); writing a one to a PINx bit toggles the matching PORTx bit. PUD in MCUCR turns off every pull-up. Enabling an alternate function on some pins leaves the rest of the port usable as general I/O.

DDxn = 1 makes the pin an output driven high or low by PORTxn; DDxn = 0 makes it an input, with the pull-up on when PORTxn = 1. Writing PORTxn to zero or making the pin an output turns the pull-up off. Pins are tri-stated in reset with no clock needed.

Port-wise BBMx bits in PORTCR enable break-before-make: switching DDxn from input to output inserts one system clock of tri-state before the PORTxn value appears. DDxn should then toggle no faster than every two system clocks. Output-to-input switching adds no tri-state period.

Going from tri-state (DDxn, PORTxn = 00) to output high (11), or back, the pin passes through either pull-up on (01) or output low (10); PUD can disable all pull-ups where the pull-up state is not acceptable. Between pull-up input and output low, go through tri-state or output high.

PINxn is always readable whatever DDxn holds. A latch and flip-flop synchronize it, avoiding metastability at the cost of a delay of 0.5 to 1.5 system clock periods for an outside change. A value just written by software reads back after one period, so a nop is needed between OUT and IN.

In Power-down the sleep controller clamps the digital input to ground ahead of the Schmitt trigger, so floating or mid-supply inputs draw no current. Pins enabled as external interrupts, and some alternate functions, override the clamp. A high level on an asynchronous interrupt pin set for edge or change while that interrupt is disabled sets its flag on waking, because the clamp itself makes a change.

Unused pins should be held at a defined level to save current in active, idle and reset, where inputs are enabled. The internal pull-up is simplest but is off during reset; an external pull-up or pull-down avoids current in reset. Wiring an unused pin directly to a supply rail is advised against: should it be set as an output by mistake, large current flows.
Peripherals take over a pin through override signals for pull-up, direction, output value, toggle and digital input enable, plus direct digital and analog paths to the pad.

Used as clock pins, PB6 and PB7 read 0 in their DDB, PORTB and PINB bits. CLKI on PB6 cannot be general I/O. As SPI slave, SCK, MOSI and SS become inputs whatever DDB says, and MISO follows DDB4; as master, SCK, MOSI and SS follow DDB and MISO is forced in; a forced input keeps its pull-up under PORTB control. A low on SS activates the SPI slave. OC1A and OC1B need DDB1 or DDB2 set to output and also carry the timer's PWM. CLKO on PB0 is output whenever CKOUT is programmed, regardless of PORTB0 and DDB0, and during reset.

PC6 is RESET unless RSTDISBL is programmed; then it is I/O and the device relies on power-on and brown-out reset. As reset, DDC6, PORTC6 and PINC6 read 0. With TWEN set in TWCR, PC5 and PC4 leave the port and become SCL and SDA: open-drain, slew-limited drivers with a filter that suppresses spikes under 50 ns. ADC4 and ADC5 run from the digital supply; ADC0 to ADC3 from the analog supply.
Used as AIN0 or AIN1, PD6 and PD7 should be inputs with the pull-up off so the digital port does not disturb the comparator. PD5 and PD4 are the count inputs T1 and T0. PD3 and PD2 are INT1 and INT0.
PORTCR holds BBMD to BBMA, enabling break-before-make on ports D to A, and PUDD to PUDA, disabling the pull-ups of ports D to A; each PUDx is ORed with the global PUD.

An 8-bit timer with two output compare units (A and B), clear-on-compare (auto reload) and three interrupt sources: overflow TOV0 and compare matches OCF0A and OCF0B. It offers two modes, Normal and CTC. PRTIM0 in PRR must be 0 for the module to run.

TCNT0, OCR0A and OCR0B are 8-bit. The interrupt flags sit in TIFR0 and each has its own mask bit in TIMSK0. The timer clock clkT0 comes from the prescaler or from the T0 pin, chosen with CS0[2:0] in TCCR0A; with no source selected the timer is stopped. OCR0A and OCR0B are compared with TCNT0 on every timer clock.

On each clkT0 the counter is incremented or cleared, as the mode decides. CS0[2:0] = 0 stops it, but the CPU can still read and write TCNT0, and a CPU write takes priority over a clear or count in the same cycle. The CTC0 bit in TCCR0A picks the count sequence, and with it when TOV0 is set; TOV0 can raise an interrupt.

An 8-bit comparator watches TCNT0 against OCR0A and OCR0B. On equality the flag OCF0A or OCF0B is set one timer clock later and, if enabled, requests an interrupt. The flag clears when its interrupt vector runs, or when software writes a one to it.

Any CPU write to TCNT0 suppresses a compare match in the following timer clock, even with the timer stopped, so OCR0x can be loaded with the TCNT0 value without an interrupt once the clock starts. Writing TCNT0 with a value equal to OCR0x therefore loses that match, in either mode, running or not.

CTC0 = 0. The counter only counts up and is never cleared: it rolls from 0xFF to 0x00, and TOV0 is set in the timer clock where TCNT0 becomes zero. TOV0 then acts as a ninth bit that hardware sets but does not clear; with the overflow interrupt clearing it, software can extend the count. TCNT0 may be written at any time. The compare units can time interrupts.

CTC0 = 1. TCNT0 counts up to OCR0A and is then cleared, so OCR0A sets TOP and the resolution, which gives control of the match frequency and eases external event counting. OCF0A can interrupt at every TOP and its handler may change TOP. OCR0A has no double buffer: if a new value below the present TCNT0 is written, the match is missed and the counter runs to 0xFF and wraps through 0x00 first, so a TOP near BOTTOM with little or no prescaling needs care. TOV0 is set when the count passes from MAX to 0x00.

The timer is synchronous: clkT0 acts as a clock enable derived from clkI/O, either every cycle or one in N with the prescaler. TOV0 is set as TCNT0 moves from MAX to BOTTOM. OCF0B in every mode, and OCF0A outside CTC, is set on the timer clock after TCNT0 equals OCR0x. In CTC, OCF0A is set and TCNT0 cleared as the count leaves TOP (OCR0A).

Timer/Counter0 Control Register A at 0x25 (0x45): bits 7:4 are reserved and read 0; bit 3 is CTC0, choosing Normal (0) or CTC (1) mode and with it the TOP source; bits 2:0 are CS02:CS00, the clock select. All bits reset to 0.

A true 16-bit timer, allowing 16-bit PWM, with two output compare units whose compare registers are double buffered, one input capture unit with a noise canceler, clear-on-compare (auto reload), glitch-free phase correct PWM, a variable PWM period, a frequency generator and an external event counter. It has four interrupt sources: TOV1, OCF1A, OCF1B and ICF1. Its pins are OC1A (PB1), OC1B (PB2), ICP1 (PB0) and T1 (PD5).

PRTIM1 in PRR must be 0 for the module to run. TCNT1, OCR1A, OCR1B and ICR1 are 16-bit and need the byte-access order of the 16-bit registers; TCCR1A and TCCR1B are 8-bit with no access limits. Flags are in TIFR1, masks in TIMSK1. clkT1 comes from the prescaler or the T1 pin. The double-buffered OCR1A/B are compared with TCNT1 continuously and drive the waveform generator on OC1A/OC1B. ICR1 captures TCNT1 on an edge at ICP1 or at the analog comparator. TOP is OCR1A, ICR1 or a fixed value, by mode; with OCR1A as TOP in a PWM mode, OC1A cannot output PWM, but TOP is then double buffered and can change while running. ICR1 can hold a fixed TOP instead, leaving OCR1A free for PWM.

TCNT1, OCR1A/B and ICR1 are reached through the 8-bit bus in two byte accesses. One 8-bit TEMP register, shared by all the 16-bit registers of the timer, holds the high byte; the low-byte access performs the 16-bit transfer. Writing the low byte copies TEMP and the low byte into the register in one clock; reading the low byte copies the high byte into TEMP in the same clock. So write high then low, and read low then high. Reads of OCR1A/B do not go through TEMP. A C compiler orders the bytes itself.

If an interrupt between the two byte accesses touches any 16-bit register of the timer, TEMP is overwritten and the outer access is corrupted. When both main code and interrupt code use these registers, the main code must disable interrupts around each 16-bit read or write, saving and restoring SREG.

When several 16-bit registers are written with the same high byte, that byte needs writing only once; the atomic-access rule still holds. Timer/Counter1's clock source is chosen with CS1[2:0] in TCCR1B.

TCNT1 is two I/O locations, TCNT1H and TCNT1L. The CPU reaches TCNT1H only through TEMP: TEMP takes TCNT1H when TCNT1L is read, and TCNT1H takes TEMP when TCNT1L is written, so the whole count moves in one cycle. Some writes to TCNT1 while counting give unpredictable results. On each clkT1 the counter is cleared, incremented or decremented by mode; CS1[2:0] = 0 stops it, yet TCNT1 stays accessible and a CPU write wins over a clear or count. WGM1[3:0], split over TCCR1A and TCCR1B, sets the count sequence and when TOV1 is set.

An event on ICP1, or on the analog comparator output ACO, that matches the edge setting copies TCNT1 into ICR1 and sets ICF1 in the same system clock. With ICIE1 = 1 this raises an interrupt; ICF1 clears when the vector runs or when a one is written to it. The time stamps give frequency, duty cycle or an event log.
Read ICR1L first, then ICR1H (through TEMP). ICR1 can be written only in a waveform mode that uses it as TOP; set WGM1[3:0] first, then write ICR1H before ICR1L.

ICP1 is the main trigger. Setting ACIC in ACSR selects the analog comparator output instead; the switch itself can cause a capture, so clear ICF1 afterwards. ICP1 and ACO are sampled and edge-detected the same way as the T1 pin; the noise canceler, when on, adds four system clocks of delay. The noise canceler and edge detector input is always active except in a waveform mode with ICR1 as TOP. Driving the ICP1 port bit from software can trigger a capture.

Set with ICNC1 in TCCR1B. The input must read the same on four successive samples before the edge detector sees a change, adding four system clocks from input change to ICR1 update. It runs on the system clock, unaffected by the prescaler.

ICR1 is overwritten by the next event if it has not been read, so read it as early as possible in the capture interrupt; the worst-case latency depends on the longest other interrupt handler. Capturing while TOP is being changed is not recommended. For duty cycle, switch the trigger edge right after reading ICR1 and then clear ICF1 by writing a one; for frequency alone, with an interrupt handler, ICF1 need not be cleared.

A 16-bit comparator watches TCNT1 against OCR1x; equality sets OCF1x one timer clock later and, with OCIE1x = 1, interrupts. OCF1x clears when its vector runs or when a one is written to it. The waveform generator turns the match into an output according to WGM1[3:0] and COM1x[1:0], using TOP and BOTTOM for the extreme values. Unit A can also set TOP, and so the counter resolution and waveform period.

In all twelve PWM modes OCR1x is double buffered, its update tied to TOP or BOTTOM so no odd-length or asymmetric pulse can occur; in Normal and CTC modes it is not. With buffering on, the CPU reaches the buffer; with it off, the compare register itself. Only CPU writes change OCR1x, so it is read without TEMP (low byte first is still good practice), but it is written through TEMP: high byte first, then the low byte write moves both into the buffer or compare register in one clock.
In non-PWM modes writing a one to FOC1x forces a match: OC1x is set, cleared or toggled as COM1x[1:0] says, but OCF1x is not set and the timer is neither reloaded nor cleared.

Any CPU write to TCNT1 suppresses a match in the next timer clock, even with the timer stopped, so OCR1x can equal TCNT1 without an interrupt when the clock starts. Writing TCNT1 equal to OCR1x thus loses that match. In PWM modes with variable TOP, do not write TCNT1 equal to TOP: the TOP match is skipped and the count runs on to 0xFFFF. Likewise do not write BOTTOM while counting down.

Set the OC1x level before making the port pin an output; FOC1x in Normal mode is the simplest way. OC1x keeps its value across waveform mode changes. COM1x[1:0] is not double buffered with the compare value; a change acts at once.

COM1x[1:0] decides what the waveform generator does to OC1x at the next match, and whether OC1x drives the pin. With either bit set, OC1x replaces the PORT value, but the pin direction still follows DDR: the DDR bit must be an output for OC1x to appear. The internal OC1x register, not the pin, is what changes, and a system reset clears it to 0. Some COM1x settings are reserved in some modes. COM1x has no effect on input capture.

COM1x[1:0] = 0 means no action on OC1x at the next match in every mode. Non-PWM actions, fast PWM actions and phase correct / phase and frequency correct actions each have their own COM1x encoding. A new COM1x value acts from the first match after it is written; in non-PWM modes FOC1x makes it act at once.

WGM1[3:0] sets how the counter counts; COM1x[1:0] sets the output and does not change counting. In PWM modes COM1x chooses inverted or non-inverted output; in non-PWM modes it chooses set, clear or toggle on a match.

WGM1[3:0] = 0. Counts up only, rolls from 0xFFFF to 0x0000, and sets TOV1 in the timer clock where TCNT1 becomes zero; TOV1 acts as a 17th bit set by hardware only, cleared by the overflow interrupt. TCNT1 may be written at any time. Input capture is simple in this mode, provided the time between events does not exceed the counter range; otherwise use the overflow interrupt or the prescaler to extend it. The compare units can time interrupts; generating waveforms this way costs too much CPU time and is not recommended.

WGM1[3:0] = 4 clears TCNT1 when it equals OCR1A; WGM1[3:0] = 12 clears it at ICR1. That register is TOP and sets the resolution. OCF1A or ICF1, whichever register holds TOP, can interrupt at every TOP. There is no double buffering: a new TOP below the present TCNT1 misses the match and the count goes to 0xFFFF and wraps through 0x0000 first, so a TOP near BOTTOM with little or no prescaling needs care; fast PWM with OCR1A as TOP (WGM1[3:0] = 15) avoids this through its buffer. COM1A[1:0] = 1 toggles OC1A on each match (with DDR_OC1A = 1), up to fclk_I/O/2 with OCR1A = 0. TOV1 is set as the count passes from MAX to 0x0000.

WGM1[3:0] = 5, 6 or 7 (TOP fixed at 0x00FF, 0x01FF or 0x03FF: 8, 9 or 10 bits), 14 (TOP = ICR1) or 15 (TOP = OCR1A). Single slope: the count runs from BOTTOM to TOP and is cleared on the next timer clock, so this mode can run twice as fast as the dual-slope modes, which suits power regulation, rectifying and DAC uses with small inductors and capacitors. Resolution runs from 2 bits (TOP = 0x0003) to 16 bits (TOP = MAX). TOV1 is set at every TOP, and OCF1A or ICF1 in the same clock when that register is TOP; their handlers can update TOP and the compare values. A new TOP must be at least every compare value or those matches never happen. With a fixed TOP, unused OCR1x bits are masked to zero on write.

ICR1 is not double buffered: lowering it below the running TCNT1 with little or no prescaling misses the TOP match, and the count goes to 0xFFFF and wraps first. OCR1A is double buffered and may be written at any time; the buffer is copied in on the timer clock where TCNT1 matches TOP, the same clock that clears TCNT1 and sets TOV1. ICR1 suits a fixed TOP and frees OCR1A for PWM on OC1A; OCR1A as TOP is better when the PWM frequency changes while running.

COM1x[1:0] = 2 gives non-inverted PWM, 3 inverted, visible on the pin when its DDR bit is an output. OC1x changes at the OCR1x match and changes back on the clock where the counter clears from TOP to BOTTOM. OCR1x = BOTTOM (0x0000) gives a narrow spike every TOP+1 timer clocks; OCR1x = TOP gives a steady high or low, by COM1x polarity. For a 50% square wave, COM1A[1:0] = 1 with WGM1[3:0] = 15 toggles OC1A on each match, up to fclk_I/O/2 with OCR1A = 0; this is the CTC toggle with OCR1A buffering added.

WGM1[3:0] = 1, 2 or 3 (TOP fixed at 0x00FF, 0x01FF or 0x03FF), 10 (TOP = ICR1) or 11 (TOP = OCR1A). Dual slope: the count runs from BOTTOM (0x0000) up to TOP and back down. Non-inverting, OC1x clears on the match while counting up and sets on the match while counting down; inverting is the reverse. The top frequency is lower than single slope, but the symmetric output is preferred for motor control. Resolution 2 to 16 bits (TOP = 0x0003 to MAX). TCNT1 stays at TOP for one timer clock. TOV1 is set at BOTTOM; OCF1A or ICF1, when that register is TOP, is set at TOP, in the clock where OCR1x takes its buffered value.

A new TOP must be at least every compare value or those matches never happen; with a fixed TOP, unused OCR1x bits are masked to zero on write. Since OCR1x updates at TOP, a period runs from TOP to TOP: its falling slope follows the old TOP and its rising slope the new one, so changing TOP while running can give an asymmetric period. Phase and frequency correct mode is recommended when TOP changes while running; with a static TOP the two modes behave practically the same.

COM1x[1:0] = 2 gives non-inverted PWM, 3 inverted, visible when the DDR bit is an output. OC1x is set or cleared at the match while counting up and the reverse at the match while counting down. Non-inverted, OCR1x = BOTTOM holds the output low and OCR1x = TOP holds it high; inverted is the opposite. With OCR1A as TOP (WGM1[3:0] = 11) and COM1A[1:0] = 1, OC1A toggles at 50% duty.

operation.topic: Timer/Counter1 phase and frequency correct PWM
operation.text: WGM1[3:0] = 8 (TOP = ICR1) or 9 (TOP = OCR1A). Dual slope like phase correct, with the same output rule and the same preference for motor control; the difference is when OCR1x takes its buffered value: at BOTTOM rather than TOP. Resolution 2 to 16 bits (TOP = 0x0003 to MAX). TCNT1 stays at TOP for one timer clock. TOV1 is set at BOTTOM, in the clock where OCR1x updates; OCF1A or ICF1, when that register is TOP, is set when TCNT1 reaches TOP.

operation.topic: Phase and frequency correct PWM output
operation.text: A new TOP must be at least every compare value. Because OCR1x updates at BOTTOM, both slopes of a period always have the same length, so the pulses are symmetric in every period and the frequency is correct. ICR1 suits a fixed TOP and frees OCR1A for PWM; OCR1A as TOP is better when the frequency changes while running, for its buffer. COM1x[1:0] = 0b10 gives non-inverted PWM, 0b11 inverted, visible when the DDR bit is an output. Non-inverted, OCR1x = BOTTOM holds the output low and OCR1x = TOP sets it high; inverted is the opposite. OCR1A as TOP with COM1A[1:0] = 1 toggles OC1A at 50% duty.

The timer is synchronous: clkT1 is a clock enable from clkI/O, every cycle or one in N with the prescaler. OCF1x is set on the timer clock after TCNT1 equals OCR1x. Near TOP, CTC and fast PWM go from TOP to BOTTOM, while phase correct and phase and frequency correct turn from TOP to TOP-1. In fast PWM, TOV1, and ICF1 when ICR1 is TOP, are set as the count leaves TOP, and a buffered OCR1x takes its new value there. In phase and frequency correct mode the update happens at BOTTOM instead, with the same timing about BOTTOM; modes that set TOV1 at BOTTOM likewise.

Timer/Counter0 and Timer/Counter1 share one prescaler but select their clocks separately. CSn[2:0] = 1 clocks the timer straight from the system clock, the fastest choice (up to fCLK_I/O); otherwise one of four taps gives fCLK_I/O/8, /64, /256 or /1024.

The prescaler runs freely whatever the timers select, so a timer started on a prescaled clock (CSn[2:0] = 0b010, 0b011, 0b100 or 0b101) sees its first count 1 to N+1 system clocks later, N being 8, 64, 256 or 1024. Resetting the prescaler (PSRSYNC in GTCCR) synchronizes a timer to program flow, but it disturbs the other timer too if that one is prescaled. Writing TSM (GTCCR bit 7) to one holds the PSRSYNC value, keeping the prescaler in reset so both timers stay halted while they are set to the same value; GTCCR is at 0x23 (0x43).

T1 or T0 can clock its timer. A synchronizer samples the pin every system clock (a latch transparent while clkI/O is high, then flip-flops on its rising edge) and an edge detector then gives one count per rising edge (CSn[2:0] = 7) or falling edge (CSn[2:0] = 6). An edge reaches the counter 2.5 to 3.5 system clocks later.

Switch the external clock on or off only when the pin has been steady for at least one system clock, or a false count may occur. Each half period must exceed one system clock, so with 50% duty fExtClk < fclk_I/O/2; for oscillator tolerance a maximum below fclk_I/O/2.5 is recommended. An external clock cannot be prescaled.

A synchronous serial port: full duplex over three wires, master or slave, LSB or MSB first, seven bit rates, an end-of-transfer interrupt flag, write-collision protection, wake-up from Idle, and a double-speed (CK/2) master mode. The master clock divides the system clock by 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 or 128, chosen with SPI2X, SPR1 and SPR0. Pins: SS (PB2), MOSI (PB3), MISO (PB4), SCK (PB5).

PRSPI in PRR must be 0. The master pulls the chosen slave's SS low, both sides load their shift registers and the master clocks SCK: data goes master to slave on MOSI and slave to master on MISO. After each packet the master raises SS to resynchronize the slave. A master has no automatic SS control; software drives it. Writing SPDR starts the clock, eight bits shift, the clock stops and SPIF is set, interrupting if SPIE in SPCR is set. The master can then write the next byte or end the packet by raising SS. The last received byte stays in the buffer.

While SS is high the slave sleeps with MISO tri-stated; software may load SPDR, but nothing shifts until SS goes low. SPIF is set after each complete byte, interrupting if SPIE is set. The slave may load its next byte before reading the received one.

Transmit is single buffered and receive double buffered: SPDR cannot take a new byte until the shift finishes, and a received byte must be read before the next one is fully shifted in or it is lost. As a slave, SCK is sampled, so the SPI clock should never exceed fosc/4.

With the SPI enabled, the directions of MOSI, MISO, SCK and SS are overridden: MISO is an input in a master and MOSI, SCK and SS are inputs in a slave; the other directions are set by DDRB. A master sets MOSI and SCK as outputs, enables with SPE and MSTR (SPR0 alone gives fck/16), writes SPDR and waits for SPIF. A slave sets MISO as output, sets SPE, waits for SPIF and reads SPDR.

SS is always an input. Low, it activates the SPI and MISO becomes an output if its DDR bit says so; every other SPI pin is an input. High, every pin is an input, the SPI ignores incoming data and its logic resets at once, dropping any partly received byte. This keeps the slave's bit counter in step with the master, packet by packet.

With MSTR set, SS direction is the user's. As an output it is plain I/O, typically driving a slave's SS. As an input it must stay high: pulled low, the SPI takes it as another master selecting it, so it clears MSTR and becomes a slave (MOSI and SCK turn to inputs), and sets SPIF, interrupting if SPIE and the I-bit are set. An interrupt-driven master that might see SS low should check MSTR each time and set it again if cleared.
CPOL and CPHA give four combinations of clock polarity and phase. Data is driven on one SCK edge and sampled on the other, leaving time for it to settle. DORD = 0 sends MSB first, DORD = 1 LSB first.

SPI Control Register at 0x2C (0x4C), all bits reset to 0: SPIE (bit 7) enables the SPI interrupt when SPIF and the global I-bit are set; SPE (6) enables the SPI; DORD (5) = 1 sends LSB first, 0 MSB first; MSTR (4) = 1 master, 0 slave, cleared with SPIF set if SS is an input driven low; CPOL (3) = 1 idles SCK high, 0 low; CPHA (2) clock phase; SPR1 and SPR0 (1:0) clock rate.

A two-wire bus interface, compatible with I2C and, with reservations, SMBus. Master and slave, transmitter or receiver; 7-bit addresses (up to 128 slaves); multi-master arbitration; up to 400 kHz as a slave; slew-rate limited outputs; spike filtering on the inputs; a programmable slave address with general call; and an address match that wakes the part from sleep. SCL is clock and SDA data; each line needs one pull-up resistor and nothing else outside.

PRTWI in PRR must be 0. Both lines are pulled up to the supply and every driver is open drain or open collector, a wired-AND: any device driving low holds the line low, and it rises only when all release it. Every AVR device on the bus must be powered for the bus to work. The number of devices is limited only by the 400 pF bus capacitance and the 7-bit address space. Two sets of TWI timing figures apply: up to 100 kHz and up to 400 kHz.
Each data bit has one SCL pulse; SDA must be steady while SCL is high, except to signal START and STOP.

The master begins a transfer with START (SDA falling while SCL is high) and ends it with STOP (SDA rising while SCL is high). The bus is busy from START to STOP. A START sent before the STOP is a repeated START, used to begin a new transfer without giving up the bus; it behaves like START.

Nine bits: seven address bits sent MSB first, a read/write bit (1 = read, 0 = write) and an acknowledge bit. An addressed slave acknowledges by pulling SDA low in the ninth clock; a busy slave leaves it high, and the master may then send STOP or a repeated START. These packets are called SLA+R and SLA+W. Address 0000 000 is the general call: every slave enabled for it acknowledges and receives the data that follows; a general call with the read bit makes no sense. Addresses 1111 xxx are reserved.

Nine bits: a data byte, MSB first, and an acknowledge bit. The master makes the clock, START and STOP; the receiver acknowledges each byte by pulling SDA low in the ninth clock, or leaves it high (NACK) after the last byte it wants. A transmission is START, then SLA+R/W, then at least one data packet, then STOP; START followed directly by STOP is illegal. A slave may stretch SCL low to slow the master; the high period stays the master's.

With several masters the wired-AND settles both clock and priority. The combined SCL high time equals the shortest master high time and its low time the longest master low time; each master times its high and low periods from the line's own edges. Each master checks SDA after driving it; one that reads low while driving high has lost, and must go to slave mode at once to see whether it is being addressed, leaving SDA high but still clocking to the end of the current packet. Arbitration lasts until one master remains, into the data if several address the same slave. Arbitration between a repeated START and a data bit, a STOP and a data bit, or a repeated START and a STOP is not allowed, so all masters must use transfers of the same SLA+R/W and data packet makeup and count.

The output drivers are slew-rate limited and the inputs reject spikes shorter than 50 ns. Setting the PORT bits of SCL and SDA turns on the internal pull-ups, which in some systems can replace external ones.

In master modes TWBR and the prescaler bits TWPS in TWSR set the SCL period. A slave does not use them, but its CPU clock must be at least 16 times the SCL frequency. Slaves may stretch SCL low, lowering the average bus clock. In high-speed mode (TWHSR) the TWI runs from the system clock rather than the prescaled clkI/O. In master mode TWBR must be 10 or more.

Holds TWDR, the address and data shift register, a START/STOP controller and arbitration detection. The (N)ACK bit sits in a register software cannot reach directly: when receiving it is set through TWCR, and when transmitting the received value shows in TWSR. The START/STOP controller detects bus conditions even in sleep, so the part can wake when addressed. A master's arbitration detector reports a loss to the control unit, which issues the matching status code.

Compares a received address with the 7-bit address in TWAR, and also with the general call address when TWGCE in TWAR is one; a match is reported to the control unit, and TWCR decides whether it is acknowledged. It works in sleep, so an address match can wake the part. If another interrupt, such as INT0, wakes the CPU during a Power-down address match, the TWI abandons the transfer and goes idle; where that matters, leave the TWI address match as the only enabled interrupt in Power-down.

When a bus event needs the application, TWINT is set and, a clock later, TWSR holds a status code for it. TWSR is meaningful only while TWINT is set; otherwise it reads a code meaning no information. SCL is held low as long as TWINT is set, giving software time. TWINT is set after: sending START or repeated START; sending SLA+R/W; sending an address byte; losing arbitration; being addressed by its own address or general call; receiving a data byte; receiving STOP or repeated START while addressed as slave; and a bus error from an illegal START or STOP.

The TWI works a byte at a time and signals each bus event, so the CPU is free during a byte. With TWIE in TWCR and the global I-bit set, TWINT raises an interrupt; with TWIE clear, software polls TWINT. When TWINT is set, software reads TWSR, loads TWDR with what the next bus cycle needs and writes TWCR with TWINT set, which clears the flag and starts the next operation; the TWI does nothing while TWINT stays set. TWINT is not cleared by running the interrupt.

Sending one byte as master: write TWCR to send START; when TWINT sets, check TWSR for START sent, load SLA+W into TWDR and write TWCR to send it; when TWINT sets, check TWSR for SLA+W sent and ACK received, load the data byte and write TWCR again; when TWINT sets, check for data sent and ACK received, then write TWCR to send STOP. Each status check masks off the prescaler bits (TWSR & 0xF8). TWINT is not set after a STOP.

Four modes: MT and MR (master sending or receiving) and ST and SR (slave sending or receiving). One application may use several, for example MT to write a TWI EEPROM and MR to read it back, and SR when another master sends to it.

At each point where TWINT is set, TWSR holds a status code (prescaler bits masked to zero) and the transfer waits until software clears TWINT. Each code has its own set of permitted software responses and resulting bus actions; every code assumes the prescaler bits are zero or masked.

Master modes begin with START; sending SLA+W then enters MT and SLA+R enters MR. The TWI sends START as soon as the bus is free; then TWSR reads 0x08. Software writes SLA+W to TWDR and clears TWINT. After SLA+W and its acknowledge the code is 0x18, 0x20 or 0x38. Each data byte is written to TWDR and TWINT cleared; TWDR may be written only while TWINT is high, otherwise the write is discarded and TWWC is set in TWCR. The transfer ends with STOP or a repeated START; after a repeated START (0x10) the master can address the same or another slave, or change between MT and MR, without releasing the bus.

After START (0x08) software writes SLA+R to TWDR and clears TWINT, with the same TWCR values as in MT. After SLA+R and its acknowledge the code is 0x38, 0x40 or 0x48. Each received byte is read from TWDR while TWINT is set. After the last byte the receiver answers NACK to tell the slave transmitter, then ends with STOP or a repeated START; a repeated START (0x10) lets it address the same or another slave, or change to MT, keeping the bus.

TWAR holds the own slave address in its upper seven bits; its LSB, TWGCE, makes the TWI answer the general call (0x00) too. TWCR is written with TWEN = 1 and TWEA = 1 (so the own or general call address is acknowledged), TWSTA = TWSTO = 0. The TWI then waits for its address and direction bit: 0 (write) gives SR, 1 gives ST. After its address and write bit, TWINT sets with a valid code. SR can also be entered after losing arbitration as master (0x68, 0x78). Clearing TWEA during a transfer returns NACK after the next byte; while TWEA is 0 the own address is not acknowledged, but the bus is still watched and recognition resumes when TWEA is set, so TWEA can cut the TWI off the bus for a while.

In every sleep mode except Idle the TWI clock is off. With TWEA set the TWI still acknowledges its own or the general call address, clocked by SCL; the part wakes, and SCL is held low through the wake-up until TWINT is cleared, after which the transfer proceeds on the normal clocks. A long start-up time can therefore hold SCL low for long and block other traffic. After waking from these modes TWDR does not hold the last byte seen on the bus.

Set up like SR (TWAR and TWCR); a direction bit of 1 (read) after the own address enters ST, 0 enters SR. ST can also follow lost arbitration as master (0xB0). If TWEA is cleared during a transfer, the TWI sends its last byte, then enters 0xC0 or 0xC8 as the master answers NACK or ACK, drops to not-addressed slave mode and ignores the rest, so a master reading on receives all ones; 0xC8 means the master asked for more after the last byte. While TWEA is 0 the TWI does not answer its own address but keeps watching the bus. Sleep behaviour is as in SR: address recognition by SCL in all modes but Idle, SCL held low through the wake-up, and TWDR not holding the last bus byte afterwards.

Two codes are not bus states. 0xF8 means no information because TWINT is clear: it shows between states and when the TWI is not in a transfer. 0x00 is a bus error, a START or STOP in an illegal place such as inside an address byte, data byte or acknowledge bit; TWINT is set. To recover, set TWSTO and clear TWINT: the TWI enters not-addressed slave mode and clears TWSTO (other TWCR bits unchanged), and SDA and SCL are released without a STOP on the bus.

Some actions need two modes, such as reading a serial EEPROM: start, tell the EEPROM which location to read (MT), read it (MR), finish. The master must hold the bus throughout, or in a multi-master system another master could move the EEPROM's address pointer between the steps. A repeated START between sending the address and receiving the data changes direction while keeping the bus: START, SLA+W and the location, each acknowledged, then repeated START, SLA+R (acknowledged), the data with NACK, and STOP.

Masters doing identical transfers to the same slave never notice each other, nor does the slave. Masters sending different data or direction to the same slave arbitrate in the R/W bit or the data; a master driving one while another drives zero loses, and goes to not-addressed slave mode or waits for a free bus to send START, as software chooses. Masters addressing different slaves arbitrate in the SLA bits; losers switch to slave mode, enter SR or ST by the R/W bit if they are the one addressed, and otherwise go not-addressed or wait to send START. Status codes after a loss: 0x38 when not addressed (release the bus, or START when free); 0x68 or 0x78 when addressed for a write (receive data, answering ACK or NACK); 0xB0 when addressed for a read (send data, last byte expecting NACK or more expecting ACK).

Points to weigh before joining SMBus devices: every I/O pin, the TWI pins included, has protection diodes to both supply and ground, which SMBus does not allow, so the AVR supply must stay on or the diodes pull the bus lines down (sleep and power-down are fine while powered). The TWI data hold time is shorter than SMBus specifies. SMBus has a minimum clock speed, which I2C lacks: as master the AVR must keep the bus above it, since slower clocks make SMBus slaves time out; as slave, the TWI does not detect timeouts, so the bus can lock up.

TWBR (0xB8), reset 0, sets the bit rate generator's division factor for SCL in master modes and must be 10 or more there. TWCR (0xBC), reset 0, holds TWINT (7), TWEA (6), TWSTA (5), TWSTO (4), TWWC (3, read only), TWEN (2), a reserved bit 1 and TWIE (0); it enables the TWI, starts a master access with START, sets the receiver acknowledge, sends STOP, holds the bus while TWDR is loaded, and flags a write collision. Hardware sets TWINT when a job is done and software is needed; with the I-bit and TWIE set it vectors to the TWI interrupt. While TWINT is set, SCL low is stretched. Only writing a one clears TWINT; running the interrupt does not.

Compares AIN0 (positive input) with AIN1 (negative input); ACO goes high when AIN0 is above AIN1. The output can trigger Timer/Counter1 input capture and has its own interrupt, raised on a rising edge, a falling edge or either edge of the output. The internal bandgap reference can take AIN0's place (ACBG). Using the ADC multiplexer as the negative input needs PRADC in PRR cleared.

Any of ADC0 to ADC7 can stand in for AIN1 on the negative input. This borrows the ADC multiplexer, so it works only with the ADC off: ACME (ADCSRB) set and ADEN (ADCSRA) clear, and MUX[2:0] in ADMUX then picks the pin. With ACME clear or ADEN set, AIN1 is the negative input.

ACSR (0x30, memory 0x50) holds ACD (7), ACBG (6), ACO (5, read only), ACI (4), ACIE (3), ACIC (2) and ACIS1:0 (1:0). Writing ACD to one powers the comparator down, saving current in Active and Idle; clear ACIE before changing ACD or a spurious interrupt may fire. ACBG set puts the fixed bandgap reference on the positive input in place of AIN0. ACO is the comparator output after a synchronizer that delays it by 1 to 2 clock cycles. ADCSRB (0x7B) carries ACME in bit 6.

10-bit successive-approximation converter with INL of 1 LSB and absolute accuracy of ±2 LSB; a conversion takes 14 µs, and full-resolution sampling reaches 15 kSPS. Six single-ended input channels, plus two more (ADC6, ADC7) on the 32-pin packages (TQFP, QFN, UFBGA), and a temperature sensor channel. Input range 0 to VCC; reference VCC (AVCC) or the internal 1.1 V. Left-adjusted result option, free running or single conversion, conversion-complete interrupt, and a sleep-mode noise canceler.

A nine-channel analog multiplexer feeds the converter: the input pins and the internal temperature sensor, all single-ended and referred to GND. A sample-and-hold keeps the input steady during the conversion. The ADC has its own supply pin AVCC, which may differ from VCC by no more than 0.3 V. The on-chip reference is nominally 1.1 V.

PRADC in PRR must be 0 to use the ADC. Code 0 stands for GND and the top code for the reference. REFS0 in ADMUX picks VCC (AVCC) or the internal 1.1 V reference; the MUX bits pick an input pin, GND or the fixed bandgap. ADEN in ADCSRA turns the ADC on, and reference and channel choices take effect only once ADEN is set. With ADEN clear the ADC draws no power, so it should be off before power-saving sleep.

The 10-bit result sits in ADCH and ADCL, right-adjusted unless ADLAR in ADMUX is set. Left-adjusted with 8 bits enough, reading ADCH alone will do. Otherwise read ADCL first, then ADCH: reading ADCL locks both registers until ADCH is read, and a conversion that finishes in between is discarded, though its interrupt still fires.

Writing ADSC to one starts a single conversion; ADSC reads one while converting and hardware clears it at the end. A channel change during a conversion waits until that conversion ends. With ADATE set in ADCSRA, a rising edge on the source chosen by ADTS in ADCSRB resets the ADC prescaler and starts a conversion, giving conversions at fixed intervals. An edge while converting is ignored, and no new conversion starts if the trigger is still high at the end. The trigger's interrupt flag is set even with its interrupt disabled, and must be cleared before the next edge can trigger again.

With ADIF chosen as the trigger, each conversion starts the next as soon as it ends (free running), whether or not ADIF is cleared; the first is started by writing ADSC. With auto triggering on, ADSC can still start single conversions, and it reads one during any conversion.

For full 10-bit resolution the ADC clock should be 50 kHz to 200 kHz. Lower resolution allows a faster clock and higher sample rate; above 1 MHz is not recommended. A 7-bit prescaler divides the system clock by 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 or 128 (ADPS bits in ADCSRA), so a usable ADC clock can be made from any CPU clock above 100 kHz. The prescaler runs while ADEN is set and is held reset while ADEN is clear.

Writing ADSC starts a conversion at the next rising edge of the ADC clock. A normal conversion takes 13 ADC clocks; the first after ADEN is set takes 25, to initialize the analog circuits. Sample-and-hold happens 1.5 ADC clocks into a normal conversion and 13.5 into a first conversion. At the end the result is written, ADIF is set and, in single conversion mode, ADSC clears at the same time.

In auto-trigger mode the prescaler is reset on the trigger, so the delay from trigger to conversion is fixed: sample-and-hold falls two ADC clocks after the trigger's rising edge, and the synchronizing logic adds three CPU clocks. In free running mode the next conversion starts straight after one completes, and ADSC stays high.

The MUX bits and REFS0 pass through a temporary register: the selection follows writes until a conversion starts, is frozen for the sampling time, and follows again from the last ADC clock before the conversion ends (ADIF set). Write a new selection no sooner than one ADC clock after writing ADSC. With ADATE and ADEN both set a trigger can arrive at any time; ADMUX is safe to change while ADATE or ADEN is clear, during a conversion at least one ADC clock after its trigger, or after a conversion and before the trigger's interrupt flag is cleared, and the change applies to the next conversion.

Single conversion: pick the channel before starting; it may change one ADC clock after ADSC is written, and waiting for the conversion to end is simplest. Free running: pick the channel before the first conversion; change it one ADC clock after ADSC, or after the first conversion ends, and the result after the change still reflects the old channel because the next conversion has already begun.

VREF sets the conversion range: inputs above it read close to 0x3FF. VREF is AVCC or the internal 1.1 V reference, which an internal amplifier makes from the bandgap VBG. The first result after changing the reference may be wrong and should be thrown away.

Conversions can run during ADC Noise Reduction or Idle sleep, away from CPU and I/O noise. With the ADC enabled, idle, in single conversion mode and its complete-interrupt enabled, entering the sleep mode starts a conversion once the CPU halts. The ADC interrupt then wakes the CPU; if another interrupt wakes it first, that one runs and the ADC interrupt follows when the conversion ends, with the CPU staying awake until the next SLEEP. Other sleep modes do not turn the ADC off, so clear ADEN before them to save current.

Each ADCn pin presents its pin capacitance and leakage whether or not it is selected. When selected, the source charges the sample-and-hold capacitor through the input path's series resistance, 1 to 100 kΩ, into CS/H = 14 pF (worst case, total internal capacitance including stray) returned to VCC/2; the pin also has leakage currents IIH and IIL. Sources of about 10 kΩ or less give negligible sampling time; higher impedances need longer, and slowly varying low-impedance signals are best. Content above the Nyquist frequency (fADC/2) should be removed with a low-pass filter before the input.

For accurate conversions: keep analog paths short, route analog tracks over the analog ground plane and away from fast digital tracks, keep port pins used as digital outputs from switching during a conversion, and feed AVCC from VCC through an LC network. ADC Noise Reduction mode is recommended where accuracy matters, above all with a system clock above 1 MHz or when reading the temperature sensor; well-placed external bypass capacitors reduce the need for it.

An n-bit single-ended ADC divides GND to VREF into 2^n steps, codes 0 to 2^n - 1. Offset: how far the first transition (0x000 to 0x001) is from its ideal place at 0.5 LSB; ideal 0 LSB. Gain error: after removing offset, how far the last transition (0x3FE to 0x3FF) is from its ideal place 1.5 LSB below full scale; ideal 0 LSB. INL: after removing offset and gain error, the largest distance of any transition from its ideal; ideal 0 LSB. DNL: the largest departure of a code width from 1 LSB; ideal 0 LSB. Quantization error: always ±0.5 LSB. Absolute accuracy: the largest distance of any unadjusted transition from ideal, combining all of the above; ideal ±0.5 LSB.

The on-chip temperature sensor is ADC channel 8, selected with MUX[3:0] = 1000, which also turns the sensor on. The internal 1.1 V reference must be selected, and the ADC used in single conversion mode. The reading rises about 1 LSB per °C. With one calibration point at room temperature the accuracy is typically ±10 °C; two calibration points do better. The typical readings vary from chip to chip.

A one-wire, two-way on-chip debug link that controls program flow, executes AVR instructions in the CPU and programs the non-volatile memories. It emulates every on-chip function, digital and analog, apart from the RESET pin, with electrical characteristics the same as the real device; it runs in real time, at high speed and non-intrusively, configures itself automatically, supports symbolic debugging in C, assembler and other languages, and allows unlimited software break points.

Programming the DWEN fuse with the lock bits unprogrammed turns debugWIRE on. The RESET pin then becomes an open-drain (wired-AND) two-way line with its pull-up on, carrying the link to the emulator. The system clock stays the source chosen by the CKSEL fuses.

Any pull-up on dW/RESET must be 10 kΩ or larger, and none is required. RESET tied straight to VCC does not work. Capacitors on RESET must be removed while debugging, and every external reset source disconnected; external reset is not available while debugWIRE is on.

Break points are BREAK instructions placed in program memory; the replaced instruction is kept and run when execution continues. Each break point change reprograms the Flash, which wears its data retention, so devices used for debugging should not be shipped.

I/O is emulated exactly while the CPU runs at full speed; with the CPU stopped some I/O registers need care when accessed by the debugger. The link is asynchronous and locks to the system clock, so software changes of the clock (CLKPS) can break it, as can clocks below 100 kHz. A programmed DWEN keeps parts of the clock system running in every sleep mode, raising sleep current, so DWEN should be unprogrammed when debugWIRE is not in use. DWDR (0x31, memory 0x51) is a data channel from the running program to the debugger, reachable only by debugWIRE.

The MCU can write its own program Flash with SPM, loading code over any interface. SPM is off until the SELFPRGEN fuse is programmed (0); when enabled it covers the whole Flash, as there is no separate boot section. Flash is written a page at a time from a temporary page buffer filled one word at a time by SPM, and a page must be erased before it is written. The buffer may be filled before Page Erase (which allows read-modify-write) or between Page Erase and Page Write; it is addressed in any order. Erase and write must address the same page.
Put the address of that page in Z (PCPAGE) and write 00000011 to SPMCSR; SPM must follow within four clocks. R1:R0 and the other Z bits are ignored. The CPU halts during the erase.

Put the address in Z and the word in R1:R0 and write 00000001 to SPMCSR; SPM must follow within four clocks. PCWORD of Z addresses the word in the buffer. The buffer clears itself after a Page Write, on writing CTPB in SPMCSR, and after a reset; each buffer address can be written only once between clears. An EEPROM write during page loading loses the loaded data.
Put the address of that page in Z (PCPAGE) with the other Z bits zero and write 00000101 to SPMCSR; SPM must follow within four clocks. R1:R0 are ignored. The CPU halts during the write.
Z (R31:R30) addresses SPM. The low bits of the program counter select the word within a page (PCWORD) and the high bits select which page (PCPAGE). LPM addresses Flash by byte and so also uses Z0.
While an EEPROM write is in progress, SPM programming is blocked and fuse and lock bits cannot be read from software; check that EEPE in EECR is clear before writing SPMCSR.

operation.topic: Reading fuses and lock bits from software
operation.text: Load Z, set RFLB and SELFPRGEN in SPMCSR, and execute LPM within three CPU cycles: the byte lands in the destination register. RFLB and SELFPRGEN clear after the read, or when no LPM follows within three cycles or no SPM within four, after which LPM works normally. Programmed bits read 0, unprogrammed bits 1.

At too low a VCC a Flash write can fail and the CPU can execute instructions wrongly. Either of two measures avoids corruption: hold the device in reset while the supply is too low (the internal BOD if its level suits the operating voltage, or an external low-VCC reset), in which case a write already under way still completes if the voltage allows; or keep the core in Power-down sleep during low VCC so it cannot execute and write SPMCSR.

SPMCSR (0x37, memory 0x57) holds RWWSB (6, read only), CTPB (4), RFLB (3), PGWRT (2), PGERS (1) and SELFPRGEN (0); bits 7 and 5 read zero. RWWSB exists for compatibility and always reads zero on this device.
Three fuse bytes: extended, high and low. A programmed fuse reads 0. Chip Erase leaves the fuses unchanged. Programming LB1 locks the fuses, so fuses are programmed before lock bits.

Fuse values are latched on entering programming mode, and changes take effect only after leaving it, except EESAVE, which acts immediately on programming. In normal mode, power-up latches the fuses as well.

A three-byte signature in its own address space identifies the device and can be read in serial and parallel mode even when the device is locked. The internal oscillator's calibration byte sits at signature-space address 0x000, upper byte, and is loaded into OSCCAL automatically during reset.

With the Prog_enable pins at 0000, RESET at 0 V and VCC at 0 V, apply 4.5 V to 5.5 V to VCC so that it passes 1.8 V within 20 µs; after 20 µs to 60 µs apply 11.5 V to 12.5 V to RESET. Keep the Prog_enable pins steady 10 µs or more once 12 V is applied so the signature latches, then wait at least 300 µs before the first command. If VCC cannot rise that fast: apply 4.5 V to 5.5 V, watch VCC, and apply 11.5 V to 12.5 V to RESET as soon as VCC reaches 0.9 V to 1.1 V; hold Prog_enable at least 10 µs, and give no command until VCC has reached 4.5 V to 5.5 V. Leave programming mode by powering down or taking RESET to 0 V.

Command and address stay loaded during programming. A command is loaded once for many locations; 0xFF data need not be written after a Chip Erase (EEPROM excepted when EESAVE is programmed); the address high byte is loaded only when moving to a new 256-word Flash or 256-byte EEPROM window, and likewise for signature reads.

Chip Erase is required before Flash or EEPROM is reprogrammed. It erases Flash, EEPROM (unless EESAVE is programmed) and the lock bits; the lock bits reset only once program memory is fully erased, and fuses are untouched. Sequence: XA1:XA0 = 10, BS1 = 0, DATA = 1000 0000, pulse CLKI high to load the command, pulse WR low to start; RDY/BSY goes low, and the next command waits until it is high again.

Data are latched into a page buffer and a whole page is programmed at once. A: load command Write Flash (XA1:XA0 = 10, BS1 = 0, DATA = 0001 0000, pulse CLKI). B: load address low byte (XA1:XA0 = 00, BS1 = 0, DATA = address, pulse CLKI). C: load data low byte (XA1:XA0 = 01, DATA, pulse CLKI). D: load data high byte (BS1 = 1, XA1:XA0 = 01, DATA, pulse CLKI). E: latch data (BS1 = 1, pulse PAGEL high). F: repeat B to E until every word of that page is loaded; low address bits pick a word within a page and high bits which page, so with fewer than 256 words per page the top bits of the low address byte select which page at Page Write. G: load address high byte (XA1:XA0 = 00, BS1 = 1, DATA, pulse CLKI). H: pulse WR low to program that page; wait for RDY/BSY high. I: repeat B to H for the whole Flash. J: end with command 0000 0000 (no operation) loaded with XA1:XA0 = 10 and a CLKI pulse, which resets the internal write signals.

EEPROM is also written a page at a time through a page buffer: A: command 0001 0001; G: address high byte; B: address low byte; C: data; E: latch with a PAGEL pulse; K: repeat B, C and E to fill the buffer; L: with BS1 = 0, pulse WR low to program that page and wait for RDY/BSY high before the next page.

Flash: command 0000 0010, address high then low byte, then OE = 0 with BS1 = 0 gives the word's low byte on DATA and BS1 = 1 the high byte; set OE = 1 to finish. EEPROM: command 0000 0011, address high then low byte, OE = 0 and BS1 = 0 gives the byte, then OE = 1.

Each fuse byte: command 0100 0000, then the value as data low byte (a 0 programs a fuse, a 1 erases it). Low byte: pulse WR low and wait for RDY/BSY high. High byte: set BS1 = 1, BS2 = 0, pulse WR, wait, set BS1 back to 0. Extended byte: set BS1 = 0, BS2 = 1, pulse WR, wait, set BS2 back to 0.

Command 0010 0000, then the data low byte with 0 in each lock bit to program; pulse WR low and wait for RDY/BSY high. With LB1 and LB2 programmed, no external programming mode can program the lock bits; only Chip Erase clears them.

Signature: command 0000 1000, address low byte 0x00 to 0x02, OE = 0 and BS1 = 0 gives the byte on DATA, then OE = 1. Calibration byte: command 0000 1000, address low byte 0x00, OE = 0 and BS1 = 1, then OE = 1.

Flash and EEPROM can be programmed over SPI (SCK, MOSI in, MISO out) while RESET is held at GND; the Programming Enable instruction must come first. In serial mode an EEPROM write erases the location itself, so Chip Erase is not needed first. Chip Erase sets every Flash and EEPROM location to 0xFF. A valid clock for the CKSEL setting must be running; no external clock on CLKI is needed with the internal oscillator. AVCC stays within VCC ± 0.3 V and always within 1.8 V to 5.5 V.

Data in are clocked on SCK's rising edge, data out on its falling edge. 1: power up with RESET and SCK at 0; if SCK cannot be held low during power-up, pulse RESET high for at least tRST plus two CPU clocks after SCK is 0. 2: wait at least 20 ms, then send Programming Enable on MOSI. 3: when in sync, the second byte (0x53) echoes back while the third is sent; send all four bytes regardless, and if 0x53 did not echo, pulse RESET and try again. 4: Flash is written by page: load each byte with Load Program Memory Page and the 6 address LSBs, low byte before high byte for each address, then store that page with Write Program Memory Page and the 7 address MSBs; without RDY/BSY polling wait at least tWD_FLASH before the next page, since earlier access can corrupt programming. 5: EEPROM is written by byte (address and data with the write instruction; the location is erased first automatically; wait tWD_EEPROM without polling) or by page (Load EEPROM Memory Page with the 6 address LSBs, then Write EEPROM Memory Page with the 7 MSBs; only loaded locations change). After a Chip Erase, 0xFF data need not be written. 6: any location can be read back on MISO. 7: set RESET high to run. 8: to power off, set RESET to 1 and remove VCC.
The highest clock the part runs at depends on VCC: 4 MHz at 1.8 V, 8 MHz at 2.7 V and 12 MHz from 4.5 V to 5.5 V. Between 1.8 V and 4.5 V the limit rises in straight lines between those corners.

The 8 MHz internal oscillator leaves the factory calibrated to ±10 % at 3 V and 25 °C. Calibrating it in the application can bring it to ±1 % at any one voltage and temperature. Its frequency moves with both voltage and temperature; the calibrated oscillator curves show how far.
An external clock is timed between the VIL1 and VIH1 levels: tCHCX is its high time, tCLCX its low time, tCLCH its rise, tCHCL its fall and tCLCL the whole period.

On the two-wire bus tSU;STA and tHD;STA bound a (repeated) START, tLOW and tHIGH are the two halves of SCL, tHD;DAT and tSU;DAT place SDA changes against the SCL low phase, tSU;STO comes before a STOP and tBUF is the idle gap between a STOP and the next START. SCL rise and fall are tr and tof.

In master mode, parameter 6 runs from SS low to the first SCK edge and 1 is the SCK period, 2 its high and low halves and 3 its edges; 4 and 5 are MISO setup and hold at the sampling edge, 7 the SCK-to-MOSI delay and 8 the delay to MOSI going high after the last bit. In slave mode, 9 runs from SS low to MISO driven, 10 and 11 are the SCK period and halves, 12 the SCK edges, 13 and 14 MOSI setup and hold, 15 the SCK-to-MISO delay, 16 the last SCK edge to SS high, 17 SS high to MISO released and 18 SS low to the first SCK edge. Both polarities (CPOL = 0 and 1) follow the same timing.

Each byte loaded in parallel programming is clocked in by a positive CLKI pulse: data and the control lines (XA1, XA0, BS1, BS2) are set up tDVXH before CLKI rises and held tXLDX after it falls. A page of Flash is filled by alternating a low and a high data byte, each latched by a PAGEL pulse with BS1 set and held round it; a write starts on a low WR pulse, and RDY/BSY goes low within tWLRL and back high after tWLRH. Reading within a page loads the address, then pulls OE low: the low byte appears tOLDV later, the high byte tBVDV after BS1 changes, and the data lines float tOHDZ after OE goes high. The data, hold and setup times of a load also apply to reading.

In serial programming MOSI is set up tOVSH before SCK rises and held tSHOX after; SCK stays high for tSHSL and low for tSLSH, and MISO is valid tSLIV after SCK falls. Bytes go most significant bit first on MOSI and MISO, and the device samples MOSI on the rising edge of SCK.

The typical curves come mostly from simulation and from characterising similar devices made in the same process; they show expected behaviour and are not tested in production. Current was measured with every I/O pin an input with its pull-up on, clocked from a rail-to-rail sine wave generator. Power-down current does not depend on the clock chosen. Supply current depends mainly on voltage and frequency, and also on I/O loading and switching, the code run and temperature. Parts are characterised above their test limits but are only promised to work up to the frequency their ordering code gives. The watchdog's own current is the power-down figure with it enabled less the figure with it disabled.
